items.why: Clearly distinguishes the five spies who entered from the armed men and priest who remained outside.
The sequence is recoverable, but the priest taking the same items moments later makes the wording somewhat tricky.
The referent is clear, though “Whose ruler” is slightly less natural than asking whom the thornbush would rule.
Directly tests the stated cause of prosperity against a nearby descriptive comparison.
Asks for an explicit motive and cleanly separates it from the adjacent background statement about Israel.
The reason for Jotham’s relocation is explicit and the competing group appears only later.
Clearly distinguishes the relatives receiving Abimelek’s instruction from the citizens meant to hear the message.
Tests the Levite’s stated purpose rather than the incidental destination he reaches en route.
Calling the conditional wish a “request” is unnatural and makes the target less precise.
“Does something” is too vague to identify the reported action or provide meaningful discrimination.
The reported news is explicit, while the competing event occurs only after the ambush is set.
Strongly tests who the mother says will make the image versus who actually makes it afterward.
The servant’s object is clear, though the question is a relatively simple pronoun-resolution check.
Asks for the direct cause of the occupants’ deaths and contrasts it with their earlier movement into the stronghold.
Cleanly distinguishes the stated duration of the priesthood from the separate duration of idol use.
The immediate trigger is the shouting, but being overtaken is closely bundled with it and weakens discrimination.
The fig tree’s refusal is explicit, though “lose its sweet fruit” slightly paraphrases “give up my fruit.”
Tests Abimelek’s specific purpose at the doorway rather than his broader attack on the tower.
The intended object of “take it over” is clearly the land, not its inhabitants.
Micah explicitly gives his reason, and the competing biographical detail is nearby but not causal.
“The residence the Danites visit” is an awkward clue-avoiding phrase that obscures the simple route question.
The surrounding references identify Jerub-Baal, though shifting from “my father” to “the man” adds mild referential burden.
The sender and rival are both named, making this a clear and discriminating speaker-role question.
Cleanly distinguishes the priest they address from God, whose guidance they ask him to seek.
“After God punishes them” imposes an unclear sequence on two parallel statements of divine repayment.
Accurately tests Zebul’s corrective response to Gaal’s first identification.
Jotham explicitly states the desired result of listening, distinct from the parable that follows.
The olive tree’s stated reason is explicit and the later turn to the fig tree is clearly not causal.
The curse is explicitly attributed to Micah’s mother despite Micah being the current speaker.
Clearly contrasts the festival meal during which they cursed Abimelek with the earlier grape work.
The passage directly gives both reasons no rescuer came, while the attack is merely the situation requiring help.
